why: It is Largest Rectangle in Histogram with a twist: every maximal rectangle the stack finds (height h, width w) holds a square of side min(h, w), and any square fits inside one of those rectangles. Recognising the histogram behind the skyline story is the point.
hints: A square of side s fits somewhere exactly when what holds over s consecutive buildings?
Every one of those s buildings has height at least s. That is a rectangle question on a histogram: each maximal rectangle of height h and width w holds a square of side min(h, w).
Run the largest-rectangle monotonic stack; for each popped bar compute its width w and update best with min(height, w)^2. O(n).
pitfalls: Return the area (side squared), not the side length.
The square's side is limited by the width as well as the height: in [5] the best square is 1x1.
statement:
A row of skyscrapers stands along a road. Skyscraper i has height cityline[i] and width 1, and neighbouring skyscrapers touch with no gaps.

Find the largest axis-aligned square that fits inside the skyline: its bottom lies on the road and every column it covers is at least as tall as the square. Return the square's area.

Worked example: cityline = [1, 2, 3, 2, 1]

  • A 2x2 square fits over buildings 1-2 (heights 2 and 3), or over buildings 2-3.
  • A 3x3 square would need three consecutive buildings of height at least 3, but only one building is that tall.

Answer: 4. For [4, 4, 4, 1] the answer is 9, and for [5] it is 1 (the width limits it).
constraints:
• 1 <= cityline.length <= 10^5
  • 1 <= cityline[i] <= 10^9
  • The source gives no bounds ("TO-DO"); these are practice assumptions that make an O(n) solution necessary.
